# Introduction and data used

We illustrate in this post the notion of **ROC curves** using data from a head-to-head benchmark evaluation of five SARS-CoV-2 serological assays [@ainsworth2020performance].

The underlying study compared the Abbott, DiaSorin, Oxford, Roche, and Siemens
assays using a common set of well-characterized samples.
We follow @ainsworth2020performance and we have used

- **976 pre-pandemic samples** as the known-negative reference group; and
- **536 laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2-positive samples** collected at least 20 days after symptom onset.

The dataset (`supplementary_dataset2.csv`) can be downloaded [here](https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Dataset_Head-to-head_benchmark_evaluation_of_the_sensitivity_and_specificity_of_five_immunoassays_for_SARS-CoV-2_serology_on_1500_samples/12622172?backTo=%2Fcollections%2FHead-to-head_benchmark_evaluation_of_the_sensitivity_and_specificity_of_five_immunoassays_for_SARS-CoV-2_serology_on_1500_samples%2F5046032&file=23736068) and the supplementary material of the associated paper describes the preprocessing we have also followed.

## A statistical testing point of view

A diagnostic test can be framed as a classical **statistical hypothesis test**. In this medical context, we consider the null hypothesis
$$
\mathcal{H}_0: \text{``you are healthy''} \quad \text{(until proved otherwise)},
$$
against the alternative:
$$
\mathcal{H}_1: \text{``you are sick''} \quad \text{(here, infected by Covid-19)}.
$$

The presumption of health plays the same role as the *presumption of innocence* in a courtroom: we only reject $\mathcal{H}_0$ (*i.e.,* declare someone positive) when the evidence (here the assay result) is strong enough. Let $Y \in \{0,1\}$ denote the true health status, with $Y=0$ under $\mathcal{H}_0$ (healthy) and $Y=1$ under $\mathcal{H}_1$ (sick). In practice, declaring someone positive means the measured antibody level, modeled by a random variable $X$, must cross an assay-specific diagnostic threshold (cut-off) $t$. The resulting decision rule, our estimate of $Y$ at threshold $t$, is written $\hat{Y}_t$:

$$
\hat{Y}_t = \hat{Y}_t(X) = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}=
\begin{cases}
1, & X \geq t \quad \text{(predicted sick)},\\
0, & X < t \quad \text{(predicted healthy)}.
\end{cases}
$$

It is convenient to isolate the two conditional laws of $X$ given the health status. Under $\mathcal H_0$, $X$ follows $\mathcal L(X\mid Y=0)$; under $\mathcal H_1$, it follows $\mathcal L(X\mid Y=1)$. We write
$$
X_0 \sim \mathcal L(X\mid Y=0), \qquad X_1 \sim \mathcal L(X\mid Y=1)
$$
for two independent random variables with these laws. This turns any probability conditional on $Y$ into an ordinary, unconditional probability: for every threshold $t$,
$$
\mathbb P(X \ge t \mid Y=0) = \mathbb P(X_0\ge t), \qquad \mathbb P(X \ge t \mid Y=1) = \mathbb P(X_1\ge t),
$$
and we use the right-hand sides from here on, since they involve a single random variable rather than a conditional statement.

As in any hypothesis test, two types of errors can occur: rejecting $\mathcal{H}_0$ when it is in fact true (**Type I error**), or failing to reject it when it is in fact false (**Type II error**). In terms of $X_0$ and $X_1$:

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(\text{Type I error}) & = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}_t=1 \mid Y=0) = \mathbb{P}(X \geq t \mid Y=0) = \mathbb P(X_0\ge t),\\
\mathbb{P}(\text{Type II error}) & = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}_t=0 \mid Y=1) = \mathbb{P}(X < t \mid Y=1) = \mathbb P(X_1 < t).
\end{align*}
$$

In words: a Type I error is a **false positive** (the test flags a healthy person), while a Type II error is a **false negative** (the test misses a sick person). The threshold $t$ controls the trade-off between the two: lowering $t$ catches more true cases but triggers more false alarms, and vice versa. **ROC** and **precision/recall curves**, introduced below, are the tools used to visualize this trade-off as $t$ varies.

## Naming and key quantities

Naming follows the classical terminology (see *e.g.,* the [Wikipedia article on ROC curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic)). Given a fixed threshold, each sample falls into exactly one of four categories:

- **True Positive**: sick and correctly declared positive
$$\displaystyle\mathrm{TP} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=1,\ \hat{Y}_{t,i}=1\}$$ 
- **True Negative**: healthy and correctly declared negative
  $$\displaystyle\mathrm{TN} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=0,\ \hat{Y}_{t,i}=0\}$$
- **False Positive**  (Type I error): healthy but wrongly declared positive
    $$\displaystyle\mathrm{FP} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=0,\ \hat{Y}_{t,i}=1\}$$
- **False Negative** (Type II error): sick but wrongly declared negative
 $$\displaystyle\mathrm{FN} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=1,\ \hat{Y}_{t,i}=0\}$$ 

From the true status $Y$, we define two population sizes:

- $\mathrm{P} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i = 1\} = \mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{FN}$: total number of sick individuals in the study (**true positives**),
- $\mathrm{N} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i = 0\} = \mathrm{TN} + \mathrm{FP}$: total number of healthy individuals in the study (**true negatives**),

and, similarly, from the predicted status $\hat{Y}_t$:

- $\hat{\mathrm{P}}_t = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{\hat{Y}_{t,i} = 1\} = \mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{FP}$: total number of individuals predicted sick at threshold $t$ (**predicted positive**),
- $\hat{\mathrm{N}}_t = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{\hat{Y}_{t,i} = 0\} = \mathrm{TN} + \mathrm{FN}$: total number of individuals predicted healthy at threshold $t$ (**predicted negative**).

![](images/tests.svg){fig-alt="Illustration of TP, TN, FP, FN counts on a Covid-19 test example"}

[Note]{.underline}: we will reuse the same color code below, with red for $\mathrm{N}$, blue for $\mathrm{P}$, crosses for a negative test result, and dots for a positive test result.

We also define the following rates, used throughout this post:

- $\mathrm{TPR} = \dfrac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{P}} = \mathbb{P}\!\left(\hat{Y}_t=1 \mid Y=1\right) = \mathbb P(X_1\ge t)$ (**True Positive Rate**, a.k.a. **sensitivity** or **recall**): among sick people, the proportion correctly detected,
- $\mathrm{TNR} = \dfrac{\mathrm{TN}}{\mathrm{N}} = \mathbb{P}\!\left(\hat{Y}_t=0 \mid Y=0\right) = \mathbb P(X_0< t)$ (**True Negative Rate**, a.k.a. **specificity**): among healthy people, the proportion correctly cleared,
- $\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - \mathrm{TNR} = \dfrac{\mathrm{FP}}{\mathrm{N}} = \mathbb{P}\!\left(\hat{Y}_t=1 \mid Y=0\right) = \mathbb P(X_0\ge t)$ (**False Positive Rate**): among healthy people, the proportion wrongly flagged — this is exactly the Type I error probability,
- $\mathrm{Precision} = \dfrac{\mathrm{TP}}{\hat{\mathrm{P}}_t} = \mathbb{P}\!\left(Y=1 \mid \hat{Y}_t=1\right)$: among people declared positive, the proportion actually sick. Unlike the three rates above, precision also depends on the class proportions $\mathbb P(Y=0),\mathbb P(Y=1)$ (the disease prevalence), and so cannot be written purely in terms of $X_0$ and $X_1$.

The dataset consists of $n$ observations, denoted $\{(Y_i, X_i)\}_{i=1,\dots,n}$, where $Y_i$ represents the true health status of individual $i$.

## The ROC curve function

For a given threshold $t$, one would like to compute the pair:

$$
\begin{align}
\left(\mathrm{FPR}(t), \mathrm{TPR}(t)\right)
& = \left(
\mathbb{P}\!\left(\hat{Y}_t =1 \mid Y=0\right),
\mathbb{P}\!\left(\hat{Y}_t =1 \mid Y=1\right)
\right)\\
& = \bigl(\mathbb P(X_0\ge t),\ \mathbb P(X_1\ge t)\bigr).
\end{align}
$$

The **ROC curve** is the parametric curve obtained as $t$ varies:
$$
\{(\mathrm{FPR}(t), \mathrm{TPR}(t)) : t \in \mathbb{R}\}.
$$

In practice, the estimation is performed using empirical counterparts. For each threshold $t$, we compute:
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}}(t) = \frac{1}{\mathrm{N}} \sum_{i: Y_i=0} \mathbb{1}\{X_i \geq t\}, \quad
\widehat{\mathrm{TPR}}(t) = \frac{1}{\mathrm{P}} \sum_{i: Y_i=1} \mathbb{1}\{X_i \geq t\}.
$$

### Properties

:::: {#lem-roc-endpoints}

# ROC endpoints

Assume that $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite. Then, for the threshold rule $\hat Y_t(X)=\mathbb 1\{X\ge t\}$, the ROC curve has the limiting endpoints:

$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to+\infty}
\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr)
=(0,0)
}
$$
and
$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to-\infty}
\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr)
=(1,1).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-roc-endpoints')"}

[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-roc-endpoints .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}

:::

::: {#proof-content-lem-roc-endpoints .proof-content}

**Step 1: Limit as $t\to+\infty$**

By definition,
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(t)
=
\mathbb P(X_0\ge t),
\qquad
\mathrm{TPR}(t)
=
\mathbb P(X_1\ge t).
$$

Since $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite,
$$
\lim_{t\to+\infty}
\mathbb P(X_y\ge t)=0,
\qquad y\in\{0,1\}.
$$

Therefore,
$$
\lim_{t\to+\infty}\mathrm{FPR}(t)=0,
\qquad
\lim_{t\to+\infty}\mathrm{TPR}(t)=0,
$$
and hence
$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to+\infty}
\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr)
=(0,0).
}
$$

**Step 2: Limit as $t\to-\infty$**

Similarly,
$$
\mathbb P(X_y\ge t)\longrightarrow 1
\qquad\text{as }t\to-\infty,
\qquad y\in\{0,1\},
$$
because $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite.

Thus,
$$
\lim_{t\to-\infty}\mathrm{FPR}(t)=1,
\qquad
\lim_{t\to-\infty}\mathrm{TPR}(t)=1,
$$
and therefore
$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to-\infty}
\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr)
=(1,1).
}
$$

:::

::::

:::: {#thm-roc-monotonicity}
# Monotonicity of ROC curves

For the threshold rule $\hat Y_t(X)=\mathbb 1\{X\ge t\}$, both $\mathrm{TPR}(\cdot)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(\cdot)$ are non-increasing in the threshold: for any $t_1,t_2\in\mathbb R$ with $t_1<t_2$,

$$
\mathrm{TPR}(t_1) \geq \mathrm{TPR}(t_2) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{FPR}(t_1) \geq \mathrm{FPR}(t_2).
$$
::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-monotonicity')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-monotonicity .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-monotonicity .proof-content}

Recall that $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)$.

Fix $t_1<t_2$. Then $X\ge t_2$ implies $X\ge t_1$, i.e., the event $\{X\ge t_2\}$ is contained in $\{X\ge t_1\}$; this holds whether $X$ is replaced by $X_0$ or $X_1$. By monotonicity of probability,
$$
\mathbb P(X_1\ge t_2) \le \mathbb P(X_1\ge t_1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb P(X_0\ge t_2) \le \mathbb P(X_0\ge t_1),
$$
that is,
$$
\mathrm{TPR}(t_1) \geq \mathrm{TPR}(t_2) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{FPR}(t_1) \geq \mathrm{FPR}(t_2).
$$

:::
::::

### Ideal case: perfect separation

The ideal case occurs when the measured antibody level $X$ **perfectly separates** the two health-status classes. In other words, there exists a threshold $t^\star\in\mathbb{R}$ such that individuals with $Y=0$ are always classified as healthy, while individuals with $Y=1$ are always classified as sick.

:::: {#thm-perfect-separation}

# ROC curve under perfect separation

Suppose that there exists a threshold $t^\star\in\mathbb{R}$ such that, for $\hat{Y}_t = \hat{Y}_t(X) = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$,

$$
\mathbb P(X_0\ge t^\star)=0,
\qquad
\mathbb P(X_1\ge t^\star)=1,
$$

i.e., healthy individuals always score below $t^\star$, and sick individuals always score at or above $t^\star$. Then,

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star)=0,
\qquad
\mathrm{TPR}(t^\star)=1,
}
$$

and consequently the ROC curve passes through the upper-left corner $(0,1)$, in addition to the two universal endpoints $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ established above.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-perfect-separation')"}

[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-perfect-separation .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}

:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-perfect-separation .proof-content}

By definition, $\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star)=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t^\star)$, which is $0$ by the perfect-separation assumption:

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star)=0.
}
$$

Similarly, $\mathrm{TPR}(t^\star)=\mathbb P(X_1\ge t^\star)$, which is $1$ by assumption:

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{TPR}(t^\star)=1.
}
$$

Thus the threshold $t^\star$ yields the ROC operating point $\left(\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star),\mathrm{TPR}(t^\star)\right) = (0,1)$: the upper-left corner of the ROC space, representing perfect discrimination.

:::

::::

### Random guessing example

Random guessing corresponds to the situation in which the measured antibody level $X$ carries **no information** about the true health status $Y$. Formally, the conditional distributions of $X$ are identical under the two health statuses, i.e., $X_0$ and $X_1$ have the same law:
$$
X_0 \ \stackrel{d}{=}\ X_1.
$$

In other words, knowing whether an individual is healthy ($Y=0$) or sick ($Y=1$) does not change the distribution of the measured antibody level.

:::: {#thm-random-guessing}

# ROC curve under random guessing

Suppose that
$$
X_0 \ \stackrel{d}{=}\ X_1,
$$
and consider the threshold decision rule
$$
\hat{Y}_t(X)
=
\mathbb{1}\{X\geq t\},
\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

Then, for every threshold $t\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)
}.
$$

Consequently, the ROC curve is included in the diagonal line
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{TPR}=\mathrm{FPR}.
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-random-guessing')"}

[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-random-guessing .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}

:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-random-guessing .proof-content}

Two random variables equal in distribution assign the same probability to every event, so $X_0\stackrel{d}{=}X_1$ gives, for every threshold $t\in\mathbb R$,
$$
\mathbb P(X_0\ge t) = \mathbb P(X_1\ge t).
$$

Since $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)$ and $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)$, this is exactly
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{FPR}(t)
=
\mathrm{TPR}(t)
\quad\text{for all }t\in\mathbb{R}.
}
$$

Thus, as the threshold $t$ varies, every point $\left(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\right)$ lies on the diagonal $\mathrm{TPR}=\mathrm{FPR}$.

:::

::::

### Gaussian case

:::: {#thm-gaussian-roc}

# ROC curve for two Gaussian health-status classes

Consider two health-status classes with unit variance:
$$
X_0
\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0,1),
\qquad
X_1
\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1,1),
$$
where $\mu_1>\mu_0$, and consider the threshold decision rule $\hat{Y}_t(X) = \mathbb{1}\{X\geq t\}$, $t\in\mathbb{R}$.
Let $\Delta=\mu_1-\mu_0>0$ denote the separation between the means.
Then, the theoretical ROC curve has the following closed-form expression:

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{TPR}
=
\Phi\left(
\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})+\Delta
\right)
},
$$

where $\Phi$ denotes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, defined by

$$
\Phi(x)
=
\mathbb{P}(Z\leq x)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{-\infty}^{x}e^{-u^2/2}\,du,
\qquad
Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-gaussian-roc')"}

[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-gaussian-roc .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}

:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-gaussian-roc .proof-content}

**Step 1: Compute the false-positive and true-positive rates**

By definition,
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(X_0\ge t).
$$

Since $X_0\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,1)$, standardizing gives $X_0-\mu_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, so
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{FPR}(t)
&=
\mathbb{P}\left(
X_0-\mu_0
\geq
t-\mu_0
\right)\\
&=
1-\Phi(t-\mu_0).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{FPR}(t)
=
1-\Phi(t-\mu_0)
}.
$$

Similarly,
$$
\mathrm{TPR}(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(X_1\ge t).
$$

Since $X_1\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,1)$, standardizing gives $X_1-\mu_1\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, so
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{TPR}(t)
&=
\mathbb{P}\left(
X_1-\mu_1
\geq
t-\mu_1
\right)\\
&=
1-\Phi(t-\mu_1).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{TPR}(t)
=
1-\Phi(t-\mu_1)
}.
$$

**Step 2: Eliminate the threshold**

We now express $\mathrm{TPR}$ directly as a function of $\mathrm{FPR}$.

Starting from
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(t)
=
1-\Phi(t-\mu_0),
$$
and using the symmetry of the standard normal distribution,
$$
1-\Phi(x)=\Phi(-x),
$$
we obtain
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(t)
=
\Phi(\mu_0-t).
$$

Applying the inverse CDF $\Phi^{-1}$ gives
$$
\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}(t))
=
\mu_0-t.
$$

Therefore,
$$
t-\mu_0
=
-\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}(t)).
$$

Since $\Delta=\mu_1-\mu_0$, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
t-\mu_1
&=
(t-\mu_0)-(\mu_1-\mu_0)\\
&=
-\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}(t))-\Delta.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this expression into the formula for $\mathrm{TPR}$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{TPR}(t)
&=
1-\Phi(t-\mu_1)\\
&=
1-\Phi\left(
-\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}(t))-\Delta
\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the symmetry relation $1-\Phi(-x)=\Phi(x)$, we obtain
$$
\mathrm{TPR}(t)
=
\Phi\left(
\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}(t))+\Delta
\right).
$$

Therefore,
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{TPR}(t)
=
\Phi\left(
\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}(t))+\Delta
\right)
}.
$$

This proves the stated closed-form expression for the theoretical ROC curve.

:::

::::

**Interpretation**

The quantity $\Delta \triangleq \mu_1-\mu_0$ measures the separation between the distributions of $X_0$ and $X_1$ and controls the difficulty of discriminating between the two cases.

* If $\Delta=0$, then $\mu_1=\mu_0$, so $X_0$ and $X_1$ share the same law $\mathcal N(\mu_0,1)$: the two cases are indistinguishable, since
  $$
  X_0
  \stackrel{d}{=}
  X_1.
  $$
  The ROC curve consequently reduces to the diagonal line, *i.e.,* the random-guessing case described above.

* As $\Delta$ increases, the distributions of $X_0$ and $X_1$ become increasingly separated. The ROC curve therefore moves progressively above the diagonal, indicating improved discrimination between healthy ($Y=0$) and sick ($Y=1$) individuals. In the limiting case $\Delta\to\infty$, the two distributions become perfectly separated, and the ROC curve approaches the ideal ROC curve of the perfect-separation case, passing through the corner $(0,1)$.


#### ROC curve visualization

The Python code is provided below to compute ROC curves for the three standard methods describe above.

```{python}
def roc(thresholds, y_true, score):
    # Extracted from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/25009284/how-to-plot-roc-curve-in-python
    fpr = []  # false positive rate
    tpr = []  # true positive rate

    # get number of positive and negative examples in the dataset
    P = sum(y_true)
    N = len(y_true) - P

    # iterate through all thresholds and determine fraction of true positives
    # and false positives found at this threshold
    for thresh in thresholds:
        FP = 0
        TP = 0
        for i in range(len(score)):
            if score[i] > thresh:
                if y_true[i] == True:
                    TP += 1
                else:
                    FP += 1
        fpr.append(FP / float(N))
        tpr.append(TP / float(P))
    return tpr, fpr
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, auc as sklearn_auc
from scipy.stats import norm

np.random.seed(42)
n_pos = n_neg = 500

def compute_roc(pos, neg):
    y_true = np.array([1]*len(pos) + [0]*len(neg))
    y_score = np.concatenate([pos, neg])  # <-- FIX: concatenate, not add
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_true, y_score)
    roc_auc = sklearn_auc(fpr, tpr)
    return fpr.tolist(), tpr.tolist(), roc_auc

# Theoretical (population-level) ROC curves, to overlay as a dashed
# reference against the finite-sample (n=500) empirical curve above.
def theoretical_roc_random(num=200):
    # Both classes share a distribution -> FPR(t) = TPR(t) for every t.
    pts = np.linspace(0, 1, num)
    return pts.tolist(), pts.tolist()

def theoretical_roc_ideal():
    # Perfect separation -> right angle through (0,1).
    return [0.0, 0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0, 1.0]

def theoretical_roc_gaussian(mu0, mu1, sigma=1.0, num=200):
    # Equal-variance binormal model: TPR = Phi(Phi^{-1}(FPR) + d),
    # d = (mu1 - mu0) / sigma (see the "Gaussian case" section above).
    d = (mu1 - mu0) / sigma
    fpr_mid = np.linspace(1e-4, 1 - 1e-4, num)  # avoid +/-inf at 0/1
    tpr_mid = norm.cdf(norm.ppf(fpr_mid) + d)
    fpr = np.concatenate([[0.0], fpr_mid, [1.0]])
    tpr = np.concatenate([[0.0], tpr_mid, [1.0]])
    return fpr.tolist(), tpr.tolist()

x_pos = (-0.1 + np.random.uniform(size=n_pos) * 0.2).tolist()
x_neg = (0.4 + np.random.uniform(size=n_neg) * 0.2).tolist()

scenarios = {}

# Random guessing: both classes drawn from the same U[1, 2] distribution,
# so the two conditional distributions coincide (see the proof above) and
# the ROC curve is the diagonal.
pos_unif = np.random.uniform(1, 2, n_pos)
neg_unif = np.random.uniform(1, 2, n_neg)
fpr, tpr, auc_val = compute_roc(pos_unif, neg_unif)
fpr_th, tpr_th = theoretical_roc_random()
scenarios["random"] = {
    "name": "random guessing: both classes drawn from the same Uniform[1,2] distribution",
    "pos": pos_unif.tolist(),
    "neg": neg_unif.tolist(),
    "roc_fpr": fpr,
    "roc_tpr": tpr,
    "roc_fpr_theory": fpr_th,
    "roc_tpr_theory": tpr_th,
    "auc": auc_val,
    "ylims": [0.9, 2.1],
    "threshold_init": 1.5,
    "threshold_reco": None
}

# Gaussian: μ₀=0, μ₁=1
pos_gauss = np.random.normal(1, 1, n_pos)
neg_gauss = np.random.normal(0, 1, n_neg)
fpr, tpr, auc_val = compute_roc(pos_gauss, neg_gauss)
fpr_th, tpr_th = theoretical_roc_gaussian(mu0=0, mu1=1, sigma=1.0)
scenarios["gaussian"] = {
    "name": "gaussian samples with μ₀=0 and μ₁=1",
    "pos": pos_gauss.tolist(),
    "neg": neg_gauss.tolist(),
    "roc_fpr": fpr,
    "roc_tpr": tpr,
    "roc_fpr_theory": fpr_th,
    "roc_tpr_theory": tpr_th,
    "auc": auc_val,
    "ylims": [min(pos_gauss.min(), neg_gauss.min()) - 0.5,
              max(pos_gauss.max(), neg_gauss.max()) + 0.5],
    "threshold_init": 0.5,
    "threshold_reco": None
}

# Ideal: perfect separation
pos_ideal = np.ones(n_pos)
neg_ideal = np.zeros(n_neg)
fpr, tpr, auc_val = compute_roc(pos_ideal, neg_ideal)
fpr_th, tpr_th = theoretical_roc_ideal()
scenarios["ideal"] = {
    "name": "ideal: all samples are 0 from class 0 and 1 from class 1",
    "pos": pos_ideal.tolist(),
    "neg": neg_ideal.tolist(),
    "roc_fpr": fpr,
    "roc_tpr": tpr,
    "roc_fpr_theory": fpr_th,
    "roc_tpr_theory": tpr_th,
    "auc": auc_val,
    "ylims": [-0.1, 1.1],
    "threshold_init": 0.5,
    "threshold_reco": None
}

data = {
    "assays": scenarios,
    "colors": {"pos": "#e41a1c", "neg": "#377eb8"},
    "x_pos": x_pos,
    "x_neg": x_neg,
    "n_pos": n_pos,
    "n_neg": n_neg,
    "default_assay": "gaussian",
    # Synthetic values can be negative or zero (gaussian, ideal), which is
    # not representable on a log axis; real assay data keeps the default
    # log scale (this field is simply absent from roc_data*.json).
    "y_scale": "linear",
    "title_prefix": "Signal: ",
}

with open("synthetic_roc_data.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2)
```

#### Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)

The **Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)** is a scalar summary of the classifier’s discriminative power across all thresholds. Because the ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate for every possible decision boundary, its area ​quantifies the probability that a randomly chosen positive instance is ranked higher than a randomly chosen negative instance. Often the AUC is used to measure overall performance: the larger the AUC, the better the assay discriminates between the two classes.


:::: {#thm-randomized-roc}

# Randomized ROC curve

Let $X_0$ and $X_1$ be independent, distributed as the conditional laws of $X$ given $Y=0$ and $Y=1$, respectively:
$$
X_0 \sim \mathcal L(X\mid Y=0), \qquad X_1 \sim \mathcal L(X\mid Y=1).
$$
As conditional laws of a real random variable $X$, both $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite.

For $s\in[0,1]$, define
$$
t(s) := \sup\{t\in\mathbb R : \mathbb P(X_0\ge t)\ge s\} \ \in\ \mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\},
$$
and
$$
\lambda(s) :=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s-\mathbb P(X_0>t(s))}{\mathbb P(X_0=t(s))}, & \mathbb P(X_0=t(s))>0,\\[6pt]
0, & \mathbb P(X_0=t(s))=0.
\end{cases}
$$

Define the randomized decision rule
$$
\phi_s(x) = \mathbf 1\{x>t(s)\} + \lambda(s)\mathbf 1\{x=t(s)\}.
$$

Then $\lambda(s)\in[0,1]$ is well defined for every $s\in[0,1]$, and
$$
\operatorname{FPR}(\phi_s) := \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_0)] = s,
$$
so the (randomized) ROC curve $\operatorname{ROC}(s):=\operatorname{TPR}(\phi_s)=\mathbb E[\phi_s(X_1)]$, $s\in[0,1]$, is well defined for any laws of $X_0$ and $X_1$.

Moreover, at every atom $c$ of $X_0$ (i.e., $\mathbb P(X_0=c)>0$), $\operatorname{ROC}$ is affine on the interval
$$
\bigl(\mathbb P(X_0>c),\ \mathbb P(X_0\ge c)\bigr],
$$
of length $p_c$, with slope $\mathbb P(X_1=c)/P(X_0=c)$.

Finally,
$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{AUC} := \int_0^1\operatorname{ROC}(s)\,ds = \mathbb P(X_1>X_0) + \tfrac12\mathbb P(X_1=X_0).
}
$$

::::
:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-randomized-roc')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-randomized-roc .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-randomized-roc .proof-content}
Throughout, write $G_0(t):=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)$ for the survival function of $X_0$, and $G_0(x+):=\lim_{u\downarrow x}G_0(u)$ for its right limit at any $x\in\mathbb R$. As a survival function, $G_0$ is non-increasing, and it is left-continuous, $G_0(x)=\lim_{u\uparrow x}G_0(u)$, since $\{X_0\ge u_n\}\downarrow\{X_0\ge x\}$ along any $u_n\uparrow x$; likewise $\{X_0\ge u_n\}\uparrow\{X_0>x\}$ along any $u_n\downarrow x$ gives
$$
G_0(x+)=\mathbb P(X_0>x), \qquad\text{so}\qquad P(X_0=x):=G_0(x)-G_0(x+)=\mathbb P(X_0=x)
$$
is exactly the atomic mass of $X_0$ at $x$. Since $X_0$ is a.s. finite, continuity of measure applied to the nested events $\{X_0\ge t\}$ as $t\to\mp\infty$ also gives
$$
\lim_{t\to-\infty}G_0(t)=1, \qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}G_0(t)=0.
$$

**Step 1 (existence of $t(s)$).** Call $L\subseteq\mathbb R$ a *lower set* if $t\in L,\,u\le t\Rightarrow u\in L$. Fix $s\in(0,1)$ and set $A_s:=\{t:G_0(t)\ge s\}$. Since $G_0$ is non-increasing, $A_s$ is a lower set; since $G_0\to1>s$ as $t\to-\infty$ and $G_0\to0<s$ as $t\to\infty$, $A_s$ is nonempty and bounded above, so
$$
t(s):=\sup A_s\ \in\ \mathbb R
$$
is well defined. In fact $A_s=(-\infty,t(s)]$: any $t<t(s)$ is not an upper bound of $A_s$, hence lies in $A_s$ by the lower-set property; and $t(s)\in A_s$ by left-continuity of $G_0$ along $t_n\uparrow t(s)$, $t_n\in A_s$.

For the endpoints $s\in\{0,1\}$, the same set $A_s=\{t:G_0(t)\ge s\}$ is used, with the convention $\sup\emptyset=-\infty$: since $G_0\le1$ everywhere, $A_0=\mathbb R$ and $t(0)=+\infty$; and $A_1=\{t:G_0(t)=1\}$, which is a (possibly empty) lower set, giving $t(1)\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}$ with $A_1=(-\infty,t(1)]$ by the same argument (or $A_1=\emptyset$, $t(1)=-\infty$, if $G_0(t)<1$ for every $t$).

**Step 2 (level sets, and the defining inequality).** For $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$
t(s)=x \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_0(x+) < s \le G_0(x). \tag{$\dagger$}
$$

*Proof.* By Step 1, $t(s)=x$ iff $x\in A_s$ and no $y>x$ lies in $A_s$, i.e.,
$$
G_0(x)\ge s \qquad\text{and}\qquad G_0(y)<s\ \ \forall y>x.
$$
Since $G_0$ is non-increasing, $\sup_{y>x}G_0(y)=G_0(x+)$, so the second condition is equivalent to $s>G_0(x+)$; this proves $(\dagger)$.

Taking $x=t(s)$ in $(\dagger)$ yields both the defining inequality and the atom size at the threshold:
$$
\begin{cases}
G_0(t(s)+) \ \le\ s\ \le\ G_0(t(s)), \\
G_0(t(s))-G_0(t(s)+) = \mathbb P(X_0=t(s)). \tag{$\ast$}
\end{cases}
$$


**Step 3 ($\phi_s$ attains $\operatorname{FPR}(\phi_s)=s$ exactly).** By $(\ast)$,
$$
0\ \le\ s-G_0(t(s)+)\ \le\ P(X_0=t(s)),
$$
so whenever $P(X_0=t(s))>0$, $\lambda(s)=\dfrac{s-G_0(t(s)+)}{P(X_0=t(s))}\in[0,1]$ . If instead $P(X_0=t(s))=0$, the two bounds coincide and force $s=G_0(t(s)+)$; the definition sets $\lambda(s):=0$ in this case, and its value has no impact since it multiplies the null event $\{X_0=t(s)\}$. In either case,
$$
\operatorname{FPR}(\phi_s) = \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_0)] = G_0(t(s)+) + \lambda(s)\,P(X_0=t(s)) = s.
$$


**Step 4 (affine property of ROC).** Fix $c$ with $P(X_0=c)>0$, and let $s\in(G_0(c+),G_0(c)]$. By $(\dagger)$, $t(s)=c$ throughout this interval, so substituting $t(s)=c$ into the definition of $\lambda$, legitimate since $P(X_0=t(s))=P(X_0=c)>0$ there, gives
$$
\lambda(s) = \frac{s-G_0(c+)}{P(X_0=c)},
$$
a linear, increasing function of $s$, running from $0$ at $s=G_0(c+)$ to $1$ at $s=G_0(c)$. Hence
$$
\operatorname{ROC}(s) = \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_1)] = \mathbb P(X_1>c) + \lambda(s)\,\mathbb P(X_1=c)
$$
is affine in $s$ on $(G_0(c+),G_0(c)]$, an interval of length $P(X_0=c)$, with slope $\mathbb P(X_1=c)/P(X_0=c)$.

**Step 5 (AUC).** Since $t(\cdot)$ is non-increasing (its sublevel sets $A_s$ are nested in $s$, by Step 1) and $\lambda(\cdot)$ is Borel where defined, $(s,x)\mapsto\phi_s(x)$ is jointly measurable, $[0,1]$-valued, so Tonelli's theorem gives
$$
\operatorname{AUC} = \int_0^1 \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_1)]\,ds = \mathbb E\!\left[\int_0^1 \phi_s(X_1)\,ds\right].
$$

Fix $x\in\mathbb R$. By $(\dagger)$, up to the single (Lebesgue-null) point $G(x+)$, the interval $[0,1]$ splits into three sets, according to the position of $t(s)$ relative to $x$:
$$
\begin{align*}
\{s:t(s)>x\} &= [0,G(x+)], & \operatorname{Leb}\bigl(\{s:t(s)>x\}\bigr) &= \mathbb P(X_0>x), \\
\{s:t(s)=x\} &= (G(x+),G(x)], & \operatorname{Leb}\bigl(\{s:t(s)=x\}\bigr) &= \mathbb P(X_0=x), \\
\{s:t(s)<x\} &= (G(x),1], & \operatorname{Leb}\bigl(\{s:t(s)<x\}\bigr) &= \mathbb P(X_0<x).
\end{align*}
$$

On each of these three sets, $\phi_s(x)=\mathbf 1\{x>t(s)\}+\lambda(s)\mathbf 1\{x=t(s)\}$ takes a simple form:
$$
\phi_s(x) =
\begin{cases}
0, & t(s)>x,\\
\lambda(s), & t(s)=x,\\
1, & t(s)<x.
\end{cases}
$$
Hence $\int_0^1\phi_s(x)\,ds$ splits into three integrals, one over each set:
$$
\int_0^1\phi_s(x)\,ds
= \underbrace{\int_{\{t(s)>x\}} 0\,ds}_{=\,0}
\ +\ \underbrace{\int_{\{t(s)=x\}} \lambda(s)\,ds}_{=:I(x)}
\ +\ \underbrace{\int_{\{t(s)<x\}} 1\,ds}_{=\,\mathbb P(X_0<x)}.
$$

It remains to compute $I(x)=\int_{(G(x+),G(x)]} \lambda(s)\,ds$, by splitting on whether $x$ is an atom of $X_0$:

- If $P(X_0=x)=0$: the domain of integration is Lebesgue-null, so $I(x)=0=\tfrac12\,P(X_0=x)$.
- If $P(X_0=x)>0$: by Step 4 (with $c=x$), $\lambda(s)$ runs linearly from $0$ to $1$ as $s$ ranges over $(G(x+),G(x)]$. The average of a function running linearly between $0$ and $1$ over an interval is $\tfrac12$ (the midpoint of its range), so $I(x)=P(X_0=x)\cdot\tfrac12$.

Either way, $I(x)=\tfrac12\,P(X_0=x)$, and therefore
$$
\int_0^1 \phi_s(x)\,ds = \mathbb P(X_0<x) + \tfrac12\,P(X_0=x) = \mathbb P(X_0<x) + \tfrac12\,\mathbb P(X_0=x).
$$

Substituting $x=X_1$, taking expectations, and using the tower property,
$$
\operatorname{AUC} = \mathbb P(X_0<X_1) + \tfrac12\mathbb P(X_0=X_1) = \mathbb P(X_1>X_0) + \tfrac12\mathbb P(X_1=X_0).
$$

:::

::::

## The Precision/Recall curve function

The **Precision-Recall curve** is the parametric curve obtained as the threshold $t$ varies:

$$
\{(\mathrm{Recall}(t), \mathrm{Precision}(t)) : t \in \mathbb{R}\},
$$

where $\mathrm{Recall}(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t) = \mathbb P(X_1\ge t)$, as defined above. Precision, however, cannot be written purely in terms of $X_0$ and $X_1$: unlike $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)$, which are conditional on $Y$, precision conditions on the *prediction*,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \mathbb P(Y=1 \mid X\ge t),
$$
so it also depends on how frequently $Y=1$ occurs to begin with. We write $\pi := \mathbb P(Y=1)$ for this **prevalence** (the proportion of sick individuals in the population of interest), so that $1-\pi=\mathbb P(Y=0)$.

In practice, the estimation is performed using empirical counterparts. For each threshold $t$, we compute:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{TPR}}(t) = \frac{1}{\mathrm{P}} \sum_{i: Y_i=1} \mathbb{1}\{X_i \geq t\},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(t) = \frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{\mathrm{TP}(t) + \mathrm{FP}(t)},
$$

where $\mathrm{TP}(t) = \sum_{i: Y_i=1} \mathbb{1}\{X_i \geq t\}$ and $\mathrm{FP}(t) = \sum_{i: Y_i=0} \mathbb{1}\{X_i \geq t\}$, as before.

### Precision as a function of TPR, FPR, and prevalence

Since $\mathrm{TPR}(\cdot)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(\cdot)$ do not depend on $\pi$, it is useful to isolate exactly how $\pi$ enters $\mathrm{Precision}(\cdot)$: this both explains the shape of the Precision-Recall curve and warns against comparing precision values across studies with different prevalence (a point directly relevant here, since our 976 pre-pandemic negatives and 536 confirmed positives reflect the *design* of the benchmark study, not the prevalence of Covid-19 in any real population).

:::: {#thm-precision-formula}

# Precision in terms of TPR, FPR and prevalence

For every threshold $t\in\mathbb R$ such that $\mathbb P(X\ge t)>0$,

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}(t) + (1-\pi)\,\mathrm{FPR}(t)}.
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-precision-formula')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-precision-formula .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-precision-formula .proof-content}

By definition and the law of total probability, conditioning on $Y$,
$$
\begin{align}
\mathbb P(X\ge t)
& = \mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=1)\,\mathbb P(Y=1) + \mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=0)\,\mathbb P(Y=0)\\
& = \pi\,\mathrm{TPR}(t) + (1-\pi)\,\mathrm{FPR}(t).
\end{align}
$$
Also,
$$
\mathbb P(Y=1, X\ge t) = \mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=1)\,\mathbb P(Y=1) = \pi\,\mathrm{TPR}(t).
$$
Since $\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\mathbb P(Y=1\mid X\ge t)=\dfrac{\mathbb P(Y=1,X\ge t)}{\mathbb P(X\ge t)}$, substituting both expressions gives
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}(t) + (1-\pi)\,\mathrm{FPR}(t)}.
$$

:::

::::

**Consequences.**

- *Baseline of the Precision-Recall curve.* Combining @thm-precision-formula with @lem-roc-endpoints, as $t\to-\infty$ both $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)$ tend to $1$, so
  $$
  \lim_{t\to-\infty}\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi\cdot1}{\pi\cdot1+(1-\pi)\cdot1} = \pi.
  $$
  This is the Precision-Recall analogue of the ROC diagonal: a threshold so low that it predicts everyone positive achieves $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ at $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi$, the prevalence. More generally, a classifier that carries no information (@thm-random-guessing, $X_0\stackrel{d}{=}X_1$) has $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=\mathrm{FPR}(t)$ for every $t$, so @thm-precision-formula gives $\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\pi$ for every $t$: the **random-guessing Precision-Recall curve is the horizontal line at height $\pi$**, not the diagonal — this is the key qualitative difference from the ROC curve, whose random-guessing baseline does not depend on $\pi$.

- *Precision, unlike TPR/FPR, is prevalence-dependent.* Because $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)$ only involve the conditional laws $X_0,X_1$, the ROC curve is unaffected by how the study sampled negatives and positives. Precision is not: for a fixed pair

The Python code to compute this curve is provided below.

```{python}
def precision_recall(thresholds, y_true, score):
    precision = []
    recall = []

    P = sum(y_true)

    for thresh in thresholds:
        FP = 0
        TP = 0
        for i in range(len(score)):
            if score[i] > thresh:
                if y_true[i] == True:
                    TP += 1
                else:
                    FP += 1
        recall.append(TP / float(P))
        precision.append(TP / float(TP + FP) if (TP + FP) > 0 else 1.0)
    return precision, recall
```


### Precision-Recall curve under random guessing

We return to the random-guessing setting of @thm-random-guessing, $X_0\stackrel{d}{=}X_1$, and combine it with @thm-precision-formula to obtain the Precision-Recall curve at a fixed prevalence $\pi=\mathbb P(Y=1)$.

:::: {#thm-random-pr}

# Precision-Recall curve under random guessing

Suppose that
$$
X_0 \ \stackrel{d}{=}\ X_1,
$$
and fix a prevalence $\pi\in(0,1)$. Then, for every threshold $t\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)>0$,
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \pi.
}
$$
Consequently, the Precision-Recall curve is included in the horizontal line
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision} = \pi.
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-random-pr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-random-pr .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-random-pr .proof-content}

By @thm-random-guessing, $X_0\stackrel{d}{=}X_1$ gives
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t) \qquad\text{for every } t\in\mathbb R.
$$
Plugging $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ into @thm-precision-formula, valid whenever $\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)=\mathbb P(X\ge t)>0$,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Precision}(t) 
& = \frac{\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}(t) + (1-\pi)\,\mathrm{FPR}(t)}\\
& = \frac{\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}(t) + (1-\pi)\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}\\
& = \pi,
\end{align*}
$$
where the last simplification uses $\mathrm{TPR}(t)>0$ (equivalent to $\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)>0$ under $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)$), so the common factor cancels.

Thus, as the threshold $t$ varies over the range where this ratio is defined, every point $\left(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)\right)=\bigl(\mathrm{TPR}(t),\pi\bigr)$ lies on the horizontal line $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi$.

:::

::::

**Interpretation.**

- *Contrast with the ROC diagonal.* Under random guessing, the ROC curve lies on the diagonal $\mathrm{TPR}=\mathrm{FPR}$ (@thm-random-guessing) — a line whose position does not depend on the prevalence $\pi$, since $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)$ are both defined purely from the conditional laws $X_0,X_1$. The Precision-Recall analogue is instead a *horizontal* line at height $\pi$: unlike the ROC diagonal, its position moves up or down with the prevalence, which is exactly the prevalence-dependence of precision already noted after @thm-precision-formula.


- *A baseline for judging real classifiers.* Just as the ROC diagonal is the reference against which discriminative power is judged, the flat line at $\pi$ is the reference for the Precision-Recall curve: any classifier carrying real information about $Y$ must have $\mathrm{Precision}(t)>\pi$ over at least part of the recall range, and the vertical gap between an assay's Precision-Recall curve and this baseline reflects how much the assay's score changes the odds of $Y=1$ relative to the prevalence alone.


### Gaussian case

We return to the equal-variance Gaussian model of @thm-gaussian-roc,
$$
X_0\sim\mathcal N(\mu_0,1), \qquad X_1\sim\mathcal N(\mu_1,1), \qquad \Delta=\mu_1-\mu_0>0,
$$
and combine it with @thm-precision-formula to obtain a closed form for the Precision-Recall curve, at a fixed prevalence $\pi=\mathbb P(Y=1)$.

:::: {#thm-gaussian-pr}

# Precision-Recall curve for two Gaussian 

Under the model above, with prevalence $\pi\in(0,1)$, the theoretical Precision-Recall curve has the closed-form expression
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(r) = \frac{\pi\, r}{\pi\, r + (1-\pi)\,\Phi\!\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta\bigr)}
}, \qquad r=\mathrm{Recall}(t)\in(0,1),
$$
with limiting endpoints
$$
\boxed{
\lim_{r\to0^+}\mathrm{Precision}(r) = 1
}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(1) = \pi.
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-gaussian-pr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-gaussian-pr .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-gaussian-pr .proof-content}

**Step 1: Precision as a function of $t$.** By @thm-gaussian-roc, $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=1-\Phi(t-\mu_0)$ and $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=1-\Phi(t-\mu_1)$; since $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)$, @thm-precision-formula gives
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi\bigl(1-\Phi(t-\mu_1)\bigr)}{\pi\bigl(1-\Phi(t-\mu_1)\bigr) + (1-\pi)\bigl(1-\Phi(t-\mu_0)\bigr)}.
$$

**Step 2: Eliminate the threshold.** The boxed identity of @thm-gaussian-roc, $\mathrm{TPR}=\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})+\Delta\bigr)$, holds for every threshold $t$. Since $\Phi:\mathbb R\to(0,1)$ is a strictly increasing bijection, it may be inverted on both sides:
$$
\mathrm{TPR}=\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})+\Delta\bigr)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR}) = \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})+\Delta
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathrm{FPR}=\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR})-\Delta\bigr).
$$
Writing $r:=\mathrm{TPR}(t)=\mathrm{Recall}(t)$, this becomes $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta\bigr)$, which depends on $t$ only through $r$. Substituting into Step 1 eliminates $t$ entirely:
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(r) = \frac{\pi\, r}{\pi\, r + (1-\pi)\,\Phi\!\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta\bigr)}, \qquad r\in(0,1).
$$

**Step 3: Endpoint at $r=1$.** This is the threshold $t\to-\infty$: $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$, so $\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(1)-\Delta\bigr)=\Phi(+\infty)=1$, and the formula gives directly
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(1) = \frac{\pi\cdot1}{\pi\cdot1+(1-\pi)\cdot1} = \pi,
$$
matching the general baseline $\lim_{t\to-\infty}\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\pi$ established earlier from @lem-roc-endpoints and @thm-precision-formula.

**Step 4: Endpoint at $r\to0^+$.** This is the threshold $t\to+\infty$, where the formula is $0/0$ and must be handled as a limit. Write $\varphi(x):=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}$ for the standard normal density. As $t\to\infty$, both $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=1-\Phi(t-\mu_1)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=1-\Phi(t-\mu_0)$ vanish, but not at the same rate: by the standard Gaussian tail (Mills' ratio) asymptotic $1-\Phi(x)\sim \varphi(x)/x$ as $x\to\infty$,
$$
\frac{\mathrm{FPR}(t)}{\mathrm{TPR}(t)} \sim \frac{\varphi(t-\mu_0)/(t-\mu_0)}{\varphi(t-\mu_1)/(t-\mu_1)} = \frac{\varphi(t-\mu_0)}{\varphi(t-\mu_1)}\cdot\frac{t-\mu_1}{t-\mu_0}.
$$
The second factor $\to1$. For the first, using $\varphi(a)/\varphi(b)=\exp\{-(a^2-b^2)/2\}$ with $a=t-\mu_0$, $b=t-\mu_1$,
$$
a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b) = \Delta\,(2t-\mu_0-\mu_1) \ \longrightarrow\ +\infty \quad\text{as } t\to\infty,
$$
since $\Delta>0$. Hence $\varphi(t-\mu_0)/\varphi(t-\mu_1)=\exp\{-(a^2-b^2)/2\}\to0$, so $\mathrm{FPR}(t)/\mathrm{TPR}(t)\to0$, i.e. $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=o\bigl(\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr)$. Dividing numerator and denominator of $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ by $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi}{\pi + (1-\pi)\,\mathrm{FPR}(t)/\mathrm{TPR}(t)} \ \longrightarrow\ \frac{\pi}{\pi+0} = 1
\qquad\text{as } t\to\infty,\ \text{i.e. as } r\to0^+.
$$

:::

::::

**Interpretation.**

- *Recovering the random-guessing baseline.* If $\Delta=0$ (i.e. $\mu_0=\mu_1$), then $\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta=\Phi^{-1}(r)$, so $\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta\bigr)=r$ for every $r$, and the formula collapses to $\mathrm{Precision}(r)=\pi r/(\pi r+(1-\pi)r)=\pi$ for all $r\in(0,1)$ — the flat line at height $\pi$ identified in @thm-random-guessing's Precision-Recall analogue, as it must, since $\Delta=0$ means $X_0\stackrel{d}{=}X_1$.

- *Approaching the ideal curve as $\Delta\to\infty$.* For any fixed $r\in(0,1)$, $\Phi^{-1}(r)$ is a fixed finite number, so letting $\Delta\to\infty$ sends $\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta\to-\infty$ and hence $\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta\bigr)\to0$, giving $\mathrm{Precision}(r)\to1$ for every $r\in(0,1)$ — while $\mathrm{Precision}(1)=\pi$ always, regardless of $\Delta$. In the limit, the curve is flat at $1$ except for a drop to $\pi$ exactly at $r=1$: this is precisely the perfect-separation Precision-Recall curve used for the `"ideal"` scenario in the interactive widget above.

- *Finite $\Delta$: a curve between these two extremes.* For intermediate $\Delta>0$, $\mathrm{Precision}(r)$ decreases from its limiting value $1$ at $r=0^+$ down to $\pi$ at $r=1$, with the exact shape controlled by $\Delta$ and $\pi$ through the boxed formula — larger $\Delta$ (better class separation) pushes the curve upward and closer to the ideal step shape, while $\pi$ sets the height of the unavoidable endpoint at $r=1$.


#### Precision-Recall curve visualization

The Python code is provided below to compute Precision-Recall curves for the three standard scenarios described above. It mirrors the `roc()` function, but tracks precision instead of the false-positive rate — following the $\ge$ threshold convention used throughout this post ($\hat Y_t = \mathbb 1\{X\ge t\}$):

```{python}
def precision_recall(thresholds, y_true, score):
    precision = []  # TP / (TP + FP)
    recall = []     # TP / P  (= TPR)

    P = sum(y_true)

    for thresh in thresholds:
        TP = 0
        FP = 0
        for i in range(len(score)):
            if score[i] >= thresh:
                if y_true[i] == True:
                    TP += 1
                else:
                    FP += 1
        recall.append(TP / float(P))
        # By convention, precision is set to 1 when no sample is predicted
        # positive (TP + FP = 0), matching sklearn's behavior at the
        # recall = 0 endpoint.
        precision.append(TP / float(TP + FP) if (TP + FP) > 0 else 1.0)

    return precision, recall
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import (
    roc_curve, auc as sklearn_auc,
    precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score,
)
from scipy.stats import norm

np.random.seed(42)
n_pos = n_neg = 500

# Numerical guard for Phi^{-1} at the extremes (Phi^{-1}(0) = -inf,
# Phi^{-1}(1) = +inf); shared by every theoretical curve below.
EPS = 1e-4


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Empirical curves (finite-sample, n = 500), for overlay against theory.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

def compute_roc(pos, neg):
    y_true = np.array([1] * len(pos) + [0] * len(neg))
    y_score = np.concatenate([pos, neg])
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_true, y_score)
    roc_auc = sklearn_auc(fpr, tpr)
    return fpr.tolist(), tpr.tolist(), roc_auc


def compute_pr(pos, neg):
    y_true = np.array([1] * len(pos) + [0] * len(neg))
    y_score = np.concatenate([pos, neg])
    precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_true, y_score)
    ap = average_precision_score(y_true, y_score)
    return recall.tolist(), precision.tolist(), ap


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theoretical (population-level) ROC curves.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

def theoretical_roc_random(num=200):
    """@thm-random-guessing: X0 =d= X1 gives FPR(t) = TPR(t) for every t,
    so the ROC curve is the diagonal."""
    pts = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, num)
    return pts.tolist(), pts.tolist()


def theoretical_roc_ideal():
    """Perfect separation: right angle through (0, 1)."""
    return [0.0, 0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0, 1.0]


def theoretical_roc_gaussian(mu0, mu1, sigma=1.0, num=200):
    """@thm-gaussian-roc: equal-variance binormal model,
    TPR = Phi(Phi^{-1}(FPR) + Delta), Delta = (mu1 - mu0) / sigma."""
    delta = (mu1 - mu0) / sigma
    fpr_mid = np.linspace(EPS, 1 - EPS, num)
    tpr_mid = norm.cdf(norm.ppf(fpr_mid) + delta)
    fpr = np.concatenate([[0.0], fpr_mid, [1.0]])
    tpr = np.concatenate([[0.0], tpr_mid, [1.0]])
    return fpr.tolist(), tpr.tolist()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theoretical (population-level) Precision-Recall curves, from the
# closed-form theorems (each a direct function of recall r, at fixed
# prevalence pi).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

def theoretical_pr_random(pi, num=200):
    """@thm-random-pr: under X0 =d= X1, Precision(t) = pi for every
    threshold t with TPR(t) > 0 — the PR analogue of the ROC diagonal,
    but (unlike the diagonal) its height depends on the prevalence pi."""
    recall = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, num)
    precision = np.full(num, pi)
    return recall.tolist(), precision.tolist()


def theoretical_pr_gaussian(mu0, mu1, pi, sigma=1.0, num=200):
    """@thm-gaussian-pr: closed-form Precision-Recall curve for the
    equal-variance binormal model, as a function of recall r alone:

        Precision(r) = pi*r / (pi*r + (1-pi)*Phi(Phi^{-1}(r) - Delta)),
        Delta = (mu1 - mu0) / sigma,

    with limiting endpoints Precision(r -> 0+) = 1 and Precision(1) = pi
    (proof Steps 3-4). The r=0 endpoint is a removable 0/0 singularity
    in the formula above, so it is set explicitly rather than evaluated
    numerically."""
    delta = (mu1 - mu0) / sigma
    r_mid = np.linspace(EPS, 1 - EPS, num)
    fpr_mid = norm.cdf(norm.ppf(r_mid) - delta)
    precision_mid = pi * r_mid / (pi * r_mid + (1 - pi) * fpr_mid)
    precision_mid = np.clip(precision_mid, 0.0, 1.0)
    recall = np.concatenate([[0.0], r_mid, [1.0]])
    precision = np.concatenate([[1.0], precision_mid, [pi]])
    return recall.tolist(), precision.tolist()


def theoretical_pr_ideal(pi):
    """Perfect separation, as the Delta -> infinity limit of
    @thm-gaussian-pr: precision stays at 1 while recall rises from 0 to
    1, then drops to the baseline pi exactly at recall = 1."""
    return [0.0, 1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0, pi]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Scenarios
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

x_pos = (-0.1 + np.random.uniform(size=n_pos) * 0.2).tolist()
x_neg = (0.4 + np.random.uniform(size=n_neg) * 0.2).tolist()

scenarios = {}

# All three synthetic scenarios use n_pos = n_neg = 500, so the sample
# (and assumed population) prevalence is pi = 0.5 throughout. This is
# the value the theoretical PR baselines below are computed at; per the
# "Consequences" discussion above, changing the prevalence would shift
# these curves (unlike the ROC curves, which do not depend on pi).
pi = n_pos / (n_pos + n_neg)

# Random guessing: both classes drawn from the same U[1, 2] distribution,
# so the two conditional distributions coincide (@thm-random-guessing)
# and the ROC curve is the diagonal, while the PR curve is flat at pi.
pos_unif = np.random.uniform(1, 2, n_pos)
neg_unif = np.random.uniform(1, 2, n_neg)
fpr, tpr, auc_val = compute_roc(pos_unif, neg_unif)
recall, precision, ap_val = compute_pr(pos_unif, neg_unif)
fpr_th, tpr_th = theoretical_roc_random()
recall_th, precision_th = theoretical_pr_random(pi)
scenarios["random"] = {
    "name": "random guessing: both classes drawn from the same Uniform[1,2] distribution",
    "pos": pos_unif.tolist(),
    "neg": neg_unif.tolist(),
    "roc_fpr": fpr,
    "roc_tpr": tpr,
    "roc_fpr_theory": fpr_th,
    "roc_tpr_theory": tpr_th,
    "auc": auc_val,
    "pr_recall": recall,
    "pr_precision": precision,
    "pr_recall_theory": recall_th,
    "pr_precision_theory": precision_th,
    "ap": ap_val,
    "prevalence": pi,
    "ylims": [0.9, 2.1],
    "threshold_init": 1.5,
    "threshold_reco": None,
}

# Gaussian: μ₀=0, μ₁=1
pos_gauss = np.random.normal(1, 1, n_pos)
neg_gauss = np.random.normal(0, 1, n_neg)
fpr, tpr, auc_val = compute_roc(pos_gauss, neg_gauss)
recall, precision, ap_val = compute_pr(pos_gauss, neg_gauss)
fpr_th, tpr_th = theoretical_roc_gaussian(mu0=0, mu1=1, sigma=1.0)
recall_th, precision_th = theoretical_pr_gaussian(mu0=0, mu1=1, pi=pi, sigma=1.0)
scenarios["gaussian"] = {
    "name": "gaussian samples with μ₀=0 and μ₁=1",
    "pos": pos_gauss.tolist(),
    "neg": neg_gauss.tolist(),
    "roc_fpr": fpr,
    "roc_tpr": tpr,
    "roc_fpr_theory": fpr_th,
    "roc_tpr_theory": tpr_th,
    "auc": auc_val,
    "pr_recall": recall,
    "pr_precision": precision,
    "pr_recall_theory": recall_th,
    "pr_precision_theory": precision_th,
    "ap": ap_val,
    "prevalence": pi,
    "ylims": [min(pos_gauss.min(), neg_gauss.min()) - 0.5,
              max(pos_gauss.max(), neg_gauss.max()) + 0.5],
    "threshold_init": 0.5,
    "threshold_reco": None,
}

# Ideal: perfect separation
pos_ideal = np.ones(n_pos)
neg_ideal = np.zeros(n_neg)
fpr, tpr, auc_val = compute_roc(pos_ideal, neg_ideal)
recall, precision, ap_val = compute_pr(pos_ideal, neg_ideal)
fpr_th, tpr_th = theoretical_roc_ideal()
recall_th, precision_th = theoretical_pr_ideal(pi)
scenarios["ideal"] = {
    "name": "ideal: all samples are 0 from class 0 and 1 from class 1",
    "pos": pos_ideal.tolist(),
    "neg": neg_ideal.tolist(),
    "roc_fpr": fpr,
    "roc_tpr": tpr,
    "roc_fpr_theory": fpr_th,
    "roc_tpr_theory": tpr_th,
    "auc": auc_val,
    "pr_recall": recall,
    "pr_precision": precision,
    "pr_recall_theory": recall_th,
    "pr_precision_theory": precision_th,
    "ap": ap_val,
    "prevalence": pi,
    "ylims": [-0.1, 1.1],
    "threshold_init": 0.5,
    "threshold_reco": None,
}

data = {
    "assays": scenarios,
    "colors": {"pos": "#e41a1c", "neg": "#377eb8"},
    "x_pos": x_pos,
    "x_neg": x_neg,
    "n_pos": n_pos,
    "n_neg": n_neg,
    "default_assay": "gaussian",
    "y_scale": "linear",
    "title_prefix": "Signal: ",
}

with open("synthetic_roc_data.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2)
```

## Data Preprocessing

The dataset (`supplementary_dataset2.csv`) contains the sample-level results used in the benchmark study. It includes assay measurements along with sample-collection information and timing variables such as days since symptom onset.

The primary cohort is defined by the paper as laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection with a specimen collected **at least 20 days after symptom onset**, de-duplicated by participant so that only the latest qualifying sample per person is retained.

The primary benchmark cohort is constructed in three steps:

1. Select the study populations used in the primary analysis;
2. Apply the study-specific eligibility criteria and retain the latest qualifying sample per participant;
3. Clean assay measurements and retain samples with complete results across all five assays.


For our Covid-19 study, the dataset hence comprises $n = 1512$ observations. Among these, we identified:

- $\mathrm{P} = 536$ (**true positives**),
- $\mathrm{N} = 976$ (**true negatives**).



The details of the pre-processing step are implemented in the following code environment.



```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib

name = "Set1"

cmap = matplotlib.colormaps[name]  # type: matplotlib.colors.ListedColormap
colors = cmap.colors  # type: list

raw_df = pd.read_csv(
    "supplementary_dataset2.csv",
    comment="#",
    na_values=["n/a", "NA", "NaN"],
)

non_sars_cov2 = raw_df[
    ~raw_df["samplecollection"].eq("obb_negatives")
    & raw_df["diseaseseverity"].str.contains(
        "MERS|coronavirus|respiratory|convalescent|seasonal|other",
        case=False,
        na=False
    )
]
raw_df = raw_df.drop(non_sars_cov2.index).copy()

# THEN define covid_status
raw_df["covid_status"] = np.where(
    raw_df["samplecollection"].eq("obb_negatives"),
    "Negative",
    "Positive"
)

raw_df.head()

assay_cols = [
    "abbott_result",
    "diasorin_result",
    "oxford_result",
    "roche_result",
    "siemens_result",
]

def assay_to_numeric(x):
    if pd.isna(x):
        return np.nan

    x = str(x).strip()

    try:
        if x.startswith("<"):
            # e.g., <3.80  → 1.90
            value = float(x[1:].strip())
            return value / 2

        elif x.startswith(">"):
            # e.g.,  >10.00 → 10.00
            value = float(x[1:].strip())
            return value

        else:
            return float(x)

    except ValueError:
        return np.nan

# Study populations used in the primary benchmark
df = raw_df[
    raw_df["samplecollection"].isin(
        ["obb_negatives", "oxford_positives", "porton_nhsbt_positives"]
    )
].copy()

df["covid_status"] = np.where(
    df["samplecollection"].eq("obb_negatives"),
    "Negative",
    "Positive",
)

df["dayssincesymptoms"] = pd.to_numeric(
    df["dayssincesymptoms"], errors="coerce"
)

# Eligibility:
# - all pre-pandemic Oxford Biobank samples are negative references;
# - Oxford positives require >=20 days since symptom onset;
# - NHSBT positives are known to be >=28 days post symptom onset.
eligible_df = df[
    df["covid_status"].eq("Negative")
    | df["samplecollection"].eq("porton_nhsbt_positives")
    | (
        df["samplecollection"].eq("oxford_positives")
        & df["dayssincesymptoms"].ge(20)
    )
].copy()

# print("Eligible cohort before de-duplication:")
# print(eligible_df["covid_status"].value_counts())

# print("\nEligible positive cohorts:")
# print(
#     eligible_df.loc[
#         eligible_df["covid_status"].eq("Positive"),
#         "samplecollection",
#     ].value_counts()
# )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Keep the latest qualifying sample per participant
# ------------------------------------------------------------

eligible_df["participant_id"] = eligible_df["participantnum"].astype("string")

# Missing participant IDs must remain distinct
missing = eligible_df["participant_id"].isna()
eligible_df.loc[missing, "participant_id"] = (
    "missing_" + eligible_df.index[missing].astype(str)
)

# NHSBT samples are known to be >=28 days post symptom onset
eligible_df["sort_days"] = eligible_df["dayssincesymptoms"].fillna(28)

benchmark_df = (
    eligible_df
    .sort_values(
        ["participant_id", "sort_days"],
        ascending=[True, False],
    )
    .drop_duplicates("participant_id", keep="first")
    .drop(columns=["participant_id", "sort_days"])
    .copy()
)

# print("\nAfter de-duplication:")
# print(benchmark_df["covid_status"].value_counts())

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Assay-specific numeric cleaning
# ------------------------------------------------------------

for col in assay_cols:
    benchmark_df[col] = benchmark_df[col].map(assay_to_numeric)

# Values used for log-scale plotting issues around zero:
benchmark_df["abbott_result"] = benchmark_df["abbott_result"].replace(
    0, 0.005
)


# The study's primary head-to-head analysis requires a valid result
# on all five assays simultaneously.
pcr_df = benchmark_df.dropna(subset=assay_cols).copy()

df_reality_neg = pcr_df[
    pcr_df["covid_status"].eq("Negative")
]

df_reality_pos = pcr_df[
    pcr_df["covid_status"].eq("Positive")
]

# print(
#     f"\nPrimary benchmark cohort: "
#     f"{len(df_reality_neg)} negative / "
#     f"{len(df_reality_pos)} positive"
# )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Per-assay counts
# ------------------------------------------------------------

dict_results_inv = {
    "abbott_result": "Abbott",
    "diasorin_result": "DiaSorin",
    "oxford_result": "Oxford",
    "roche_result": "Roche",
    "siemens_result": "Siemens",
}

dict_results = {
    label: col for col, label in dict_results_inv.items()
}

dict_threshold = {
    "abbott_result": 1.4,
    "diasorin_result": 15.0,
    "oxford_result": "Oxford",
    "roche_result": 1.0,
    "siemens_result": 1.0,
}

assay_counts = []

for col, label in dict_results_inv.items():
    usable = pcr_df[col].notna()

    assay_counts.append(
        {
            "Assay": label,
            "Negative": int(
                (
                    usable
                    & pcr_df["covid_status"].eq("Negative")
                ).sum()
            ),

pd.DataFrame(assay_counts)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Complete-case cohort = primary Table S1 cohort

complete_case_df = benchmark_df.dropna(
    subset=assay_cols
).copy()

pcr_df = complete_case_df

df_reality_neg = pcr_df[
    pcr_df["covid_status"].eq("Negative")

df_reality_pos = pcr_df[
    pcr_df["covid_status"].eq("Positive")

print("\nComplete-case cohort:")
print(pcr_df["covid_status"].value_counts())

print("\nComplete-case cohort by sample collection:")
print(
    pcr_df

n_neg = len(df_reality_neg)
n_pos = len(df_reality_pos)

print(

positive_samples = pcr_df[
```

## Exporting data for the interactive figure

Since the interactive figure below runs client-side (via Plotly.js) rather than through a live Python kernel, we export the pre-computed sample values, jitter offsets, colors and ROC curves to a small JSON file that the JavaScript will load.

```{python}
#| output: false
import json
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors


def export_roc_pr_data(df, dict_results_inv, dict_threshold, colors,
                        seed=123, jitter=0.3, n_thresh=200):
    """Compute ROC/PR curves using assay-specific non-missing observations."""
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)

    df_pos_all = df[df["covid_status"].eq("Positive")]
    df_neg_all = df[df["covid_status"].eq("Negative")]

    x_pos_arr = (jitter * (rng.rand(len(df_pos_all)) - 0.5)).tolist()
    x_neg_arr = (0.6 + jitter * (rng.rand(len(df_neg_all)) - 0.5)).tolist()

    assays = {}

    for key, label in dict_results_inv.items():
        usable = df[key].notna()
        dfa = df.loc[usable].copy()

        y_true = dfa["covid_status"].eq("Positive").values
        score = dfa[key].astype(float).values

        df_pos = dfa[dfa["covid_status"].eq("Positive")]
        df_neg = dfa[dfa["covid_status"].eq("Negative")]

        pos_vals = df_pos[key].astype(float).tolist()
        neg_vals = df_neg[key].astype(float).tolist()

        positive_scores = score[score > 0]
        lower = float(positive_scores.min()) / 2 if len(positive_scores) else 1e-6
        upper = float(score.max()) * 2 if score.max() > 0 else 1.0
        ylims_i = [max(lower, 1e-12), upper]

        thr = dict_threshold[key]
        thr_reco = float(thr) if isinstance(thr, (float, int)) else None

        thresholds = np.logspace(
            np.log10(ylims_i[0]),
            np.log10(ylims_i[1]),
            num=n_thresh,
        )

        tpr_i, fpr_i = roc(thresholds, y_true, score)
        prec_i, rec_i = precision_recall(thresholds, y_true, score)

        order = np.argsort(fpr_i)
        auc_i = float(
            np.trapz(np.array(tpr_i)[order], np.array(fpr_i)[order])
        )

        order_pr = np.argsort(rec_i)
        ap_i = float(
            np.trapz(
                np.array(prec_i)[order_pr],
                np.array(rec_i)[order_pr],
            )
        )

        assays[label] = {
            "key": key,
            "pos": pos_vals,
            "neg": neg_vals,
            "ylims": ylims_i,
            "threshold_init": float(np.median(score)),
            "threshold_reco": thr_reco,
            "roc_fpr": fpr_i,
            "roc_tpr": tpr_i,
            "auc": auc_i,
            "pr_precision": prec_i,
            "pr_recall": rec_i,
            "ap": ap_i,
            "n_pos": int(len(df_pos)),
            "n_neg": int(len(df_neg)),
        }

    assays = dict(
        sorted(assays.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]["auc"], reverse=True)
    )

    return {
        "x_pos": x_pos_arr,
        "x_neg": x_neg_arr,
        "colors": {
            "pos": mcolors.to_hex(colors[1]),
            "neg": mcolors.to_hex(colors[0]),
        },
        "assays": assays,
        "default_assay": "DiaSorin" if "Roche" in assays else next(iter(assays)),
        "n_pos": int(len(df_pos_all)),
        "n_neg": int(len(df_neg_all)),
    }


def subsample_positives(df, frac_pos=0.1, seed=123):
    """Keep every negative sample; keep only a `frac_pos` fraction of positives."""
    pos = df[df['covid_status'] == 'Positive']
    neg = df[df['covid_status'] == 'Negative']
    n_keep = max(1, int(round(len(pos) * frac_pos)))
    pos_sub = pos.sample(n=n_keep, random_state=seed)
    return pd.concat([pos_sub, neg], ignore_index=True)


# Full-data export (unchanged behaviour, now via the shared function)
data_full = export_roc_pr_data(pcr_df, dict_results_inv, dict_threshold, colors, seed=123)
with open('roc_data.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(data_full, f)

# Teaching example: deliberately create a much rarer positive class.
pcr_df_imbalanced = subsample_positives(pcr_df, frac_pos=0.05, seed=123)
data_imbalanced = export_roc_pr_data(pcr_df_imbalanced, dict_results_inv, dict_threshold, colors, seed=123)
with open('roc_data_imbalanced.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(data_imbalanced, f)
```

## Interactive exploration: assay results, ROC curve and precision/recall curve

The widget below lets you select one or more assays (the first checked one is the **primary** assay, driving the threshold slider) and move the classification **threshold** (log scale): the left panel shows individual sample results split by true status *for the primary assay only*, the middle panel overlays the ROC curves of all selected assays, and the right panel overlays the corresponding precision/recall curves (AP stands for **Average Precision**, i.e., the area under the precision/recall curve). The dashed grey line / grey cross indicate the manufacturer's recommended threshold (Reco. point), when available. 

```{=html}
<div id="roc-interactive"
     class="roc-interactive"
     data-json="roc_data.json"
     style="display:flex; gap:10px; align-items:stretch; flex-wrap:nowrap; max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto; font-family:'Inter', -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;">

  <div style="display:flex; flex-direction:column; justify-content:center;
              min-width:130px; flex:0 0 130px;
              border:1px solid rgba(0,0,0,0.15);
              border-radius:8px; padding:8px; font-size:9.5px;
              background:rgba(0,0,0,0.02);">

    <div style="margin-bottom:5px; font-weight:600; font-size:9.5px;">
      Assay
    </div>

    <div class="roc-assay-radios"
         style="font-size:9.5px; line-height:1.25;
                display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:3px;">
    </div>

    <hr style="margin:8px 0; border-color:rgba(0,0,0,0.1);">

    <div style="margin-bottom:4px; font-weight:600; font-size:9.5px;">
      Threshold
    </div>

    <input type="range"
           class="roc-threshold"
           min="0"
           max="1"
           step="0.001"
           value="0.5"
           style="width:100%;">

    <div class="roc-threshold-value"
         style="margin-top:4px; text-align:center;
                font-size:9px; color:#555;">
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="roc-plot"
       style="flex:1 1 auto; min-width:520px; max-width:1050px;
              display:flex; align-items:center;">
  </div>

</div>
```

Now the same assays, the same thresholds, the same ROC/PR machinery — but with only 5% of the positive samples kept (negatives untouched). Watch a given assay's **ROC curve barely move** while its **precision/recall curve** (and AP) drops noticeably: exactly the effect the [ray-slope argument](#) above predicts, since shrinking $P$ raises $N/P$ and pushes precision down at every recall level for the same underlying ray slopes.

```{=html}
<div id="roc-interactive-imbalanced" class="roc-interactive" data-json="roc_data_imbalanced.json" style="display:flex; gap:10px; align-items:stretch; flex-wrap:nowrap; max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto; font-family: 'Inter', -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;">
  <div style="display:flex; flex-direction:column; justify-content:center; min-width:130px; flex:0 0 130px; border:1px solid rgba(0,0,0,0.15); border-radius:8px; padding:8px; font-size:9.5px; background:rgba(0,0,0,0.02);">
    <div style="margin-bottom:5px; font-weight:600; font-size:9.5px;">Assays (click)</div>
    <div class="roc-assay-radios" style="font-size:9.5px; line-height:1.25; display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:3px;"></div>
    <hr style="margin:8px 0; border-color:rgba(0,0,0,0.1);">
    <div style="margin-bottom:4px; font-weight:600; font-size:9.5px;">Threshold</div>
    <input type="range" class="roc-threshold" min="0" max="1" step="0.001" value="0.5" style="width:100%;">
    <div class="roc-threshold-value" style="margin-top:4px; text-align:center; font-size:9px; color:#555;"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="roc-plot" style="flex:1 1 auto; min-width:520px; max-width:1050px; display:flex; align-items:center;"></div>
</div>
```
